openers.offsets-and-banking: Not every harm a development does can be avoided. Offsetting answers with a promise to make up the loss elsewhere, by restoring, creating or protecting habitat. This chapter follows that promise from its logic, a set order of steps that runs avoid, minimize, restore and only then offset, to its markets. In the United States, developers buy credits from restored wetlands and from banks of land kept for endangered species, and newer credits aim to cut the global risk of extinction. Running through all of it is one aim, to balance losses with gains, and one dispute: whether nature lost in one place can truly be replaced in another.

nature-mkt-129.title: Environmental mitigation: avoid, reduce, then make up for harm
nature-mkt-129.text: Some 191 UN member states have laws requiring an {{ref:nature-pol-132}}, and more than 108 countries have policies for offsetting harm to biodiversity. Behind both lies environmental mitigation: applying measures to avoid, minimize or compensate for harm to the environment. In planning, it is usually guided by the {{ref:nature-mkt-130}}: avoid, reduce, restore and offset. In practice that means creating new habitat, restoring degraded habitat, or protecting existing habitat to make up for harm that cannot be avoided or reduced. The term is broader than mitigation in the climate sense, which focuses only on cutting net greenhouse gas emissions. Its usual goals are {{ref:nature-mkt-132}} or a {{ref:nature-mkt-133}} on biodiversity. The legal idea is old. In the US, the Fish and Wildlife Coordination Act of 1934 first expressed a legal duty to minimize and compensate for environmental harm. Whether such goals, and tools like offsetting, advance conservation or undermine it is still disputed.

nature-mkt-132.title: No net loss: balancing damage with equal gains
nature-mkt-132.text: In his 1988 campaign, George H. W. Bush promised 'no net loss of wetlands'. The phrase named an approach that had begun in the US earlier in the 1980s as a goal for wetland conservation. No net loss aims to balance a development's harm to the environment with mitigation measures, so that the total stays level. It has spread far beyond wetlands. It is now an objective of {{ref:nature-mkt-119}} in many countries, at least 69 by 2018. It is applied through Environmental Impact Assessments using the {{ref:nature-mkt-130}}. Lenders such as the International Finance Corporation require it on projects they co-finance. The record is sobering. A study of US {{ref:nature-mkt-124}} found it was producing a net loss of wetland area nationally. In one scheme in Victoria, Australia, up to 86% of offsets did not make up for lost native vegetation. Part of the problem is measurement: there is no agreed metric for losses and gains, and baselines are often undefined. Views divide sharply. Some reject no net loss as impossible or unacceptable for ecological, social or cultural reasons. Others see it as a way to reconcile development with conservation.

nature-mkt-130.title: The mitigation hierarchy: offsetting comes last
nature-mkt-130.text: Offsetting is the 'final resort'. The mitigation hierarchy sets out the steps a project takes, in order, to shrink its harm to the environment until none remains: avoid, minimize, restore, then offset. Avoiding harm comes first and is widely seen as the most important. Minimizing reduces the harm that cannot be avoided. Restoring helps damaged ecosystems recover. Offsetting compensates for whatever harm is left. The sequence is commonly built into Environmental Impact Assessment and licensing rules, and some jurisdictions require it by law. France writes it into law as the ERC sequence: avoid, reduce, compensate. Versions have been proposed for waste, food waste, energy and carbon, along with extensions such as the Mitigation and Conservation Hierarchy.

nature-mkt-119.title: Biodiversity offsetting: repaying nature somewhere else
nature-mkt-119.text: Since February 2024, developers in England must show a 10% gain in biodiversity to get planning permission. That rule, Biodiversity Net Gain, is a demanding form of biodiversity offsetting. This is a system used mainly by planning authorities and developers to fully compensate for the harm a development does to biodiversity. Offsets are measurable conservation gains designed to make up for significant harm left over after prevention and mitigation. They are the last step of the mitigation hierarchy: harm must first be avoided, minimized and reversed. The aim is no net loss of biodiversity, ideally a net gain. Practitioners measure the amount, type and quality of habitat a project will damage. Then they find {{ref:nature-mkt-122}}, land where the same can be re-created. Offsets must also show additionality, a gain that would not have happened anyway. The idea has spread. As of 2019, over 100 countries had or were developing offset policies, and more than 37 required offsets by law. The evidence is mixed. Offsets work better in simpler habitats that recover fast, such as wetlands, and one review found about one-third of policies and offsets reported achieving no net loss. Critics call offsetting a 'license to trash' that legitimizes habitat destruction. They doubt that biodiversity in one place can be swapped for biodiversity elsewhere. Supporters and opponents still disagree on whether offsets are feasible or ethical.

nature-mkt-120.title: Biodiversity banking: turning offsets into tradable credits
nature-mkt-120.text: Filling in ditches to bring back a swamp can earn money, if it happens at a biodiversity bank. Biodiversity banking is a market-based form of offsetting. Gains made at a bank site, such as reintroducing native plants or removing invasive species, become credits that developers can buy to offset their damage. Credits count only for gains that would not otherwise happen. Because they are created in advance and away from the development, offsets become tradable assets. The practice goes by several names, such as habitat banking or biodiversity trading, depending on what is conserved and where. It grew out of US wetland {{ref:nature-mkt-124}} in the 1980s, itself a product of the no net loss policies of the 1970s Clean Water Act. A bank's land is usually locked in by a {{ref:nature-mkt-126}} or covenant that binds future owners, often with a trust fund for long-term care. More than 100 countries require offsetting, but banking is less widespread. A 2006 analysis of Canadian habitat banking found 25% of projects achieved no net loss of habitat productivity and 12% a net gain.

nature-mkt-124.title: Wetland mitigation banks: restore first, sell credits later
nature-mkt-124.text: More than 1200 mitigation banks were operating in the United States by 2024, with 750,000 credits approved. Mitigation banking is a market of debits and credits in which wetlands are restored, created or enhanced to make up for unavoidable damage to wetlands elsewhere. A bank does its wetland work before the damage it compensates for, and the results become credits that developers can buy. The system grew from compensation rules under section 404 of the {{ref:nature-pol-155}}, which aim at 'no net loss of wetlands'. The first banks appeared in the early 1980s, following 1983 guidance from the US Fish and Wildlife Service. Regulators often require more habitat than is damaged, a mitigation ratio that serves the public interest. Credits are released in stages as a bank meets milestones over an establishment period of about 10 to 12 years. Even so, studies suggest a significant share of compensation sites fail to meet administrative and ecological performance standards.

nature-mkt-127.title: Conservation banks: credits for endangered species
nature-mkt-127.text: A credit can cost $1500 to cover harm to a Gopher Tortoise, or $325,000 to preserve a vernal pool, a seasonal pond. Such credits come from conservation banking, which offsets harm to species protected under the US {{ref:nature-pol-159}}. Conservation banks are permanently protected parcels of land managed to keep endangered species and their habitat alive. A developer who must harm a protected species can buy credits from a bank instead of protecting small patches itself. Pooling makes sense: larger reserves give better habitat and connections than small isolated patches, and cost less to maintain. California created the first conservation bank in 1995 and leads with over 30; the nation's 130 banks protect over 160,000 acres. Credit prices are set largely by supply and demand. Unlike wetland mitigation banking, conservation banking does not require no net loss.

nature-mkt-135.title: Safe harbor agreements: rewarding landowners who help rare species
nature-mkt-135.text: In 1995 the Environmental Defense Fund designed a plan to give landowners incentives to help endangered species. Developed into policy under the Clinton administration, it became the Safe Harbor Agreement. In this voluntary US deal, a landowner improves land for a species listed as threatened or endangered under the Endangered Species Act. In return, the landowner is allowed some future harm to that species. Unlike a habitat conservation plan, the activities it covers are designed to protect species. In 2024 it was merged with another program into Conservation Benefits Agreements.

nature-mkt-128.title: Biodiversity Impact Credits: pricing a lower risk of extinction
nature-mkt-128.text: Restoring one threatened species from near zero earns about one credit under a scheme built to cut the global risk of extinction. Academics at Queen Mary University of London and Bar-Ilan University developed its metric. It measures how interventions change the average long-term survival chances of species. For each species it adds up the change in global population divided by the current population. It targets the global biodiversity goal on extinction risk, Target 4. Critics say credits oversimplify nature and invite false green claims, while supporters point to growing private investment.

nature-mkt-121.title: Averted loss: offsetting by preventing damage
nature-mkt-121.text: Not every offset builds new habitat. An averted loss offset instead prevents ecological damage that would almost certainly have happened. Examples include setting aside land for protection, removing invasive species, or offering people other livelihoods so they stop clearing forest. The gain must be measurable: funding general research, for instance, does not count. Because the damage it prevents never happens, everything rests on {{ref:nature-mkt-144}}. Poorly designed policies can backfire, creating perverse incentives that encourage further decline.

nature-mkt-123.title: Conservation credits: habitat sold by the unit
nature-mkt-123.text: Developers can offset damage to nature one unit at a time. A conservation credit is a unit representing the cost of re-creating a piece of damaged habitat, which developers buy to offset their impact on biodiversity. Land at a {{ref:nature-mkt-122}} is valued in credits too, covering both the cost of restoring habitat and its long-term management. With a common unit, developers can buy and landowners can sell, creating a market for keeping and restoring habitat.

nature-mkt-122.title: Receptor sites: where offset habitat is made
nature-mkt-122.text: Every offset needs somewhere to happen. A receptor site is land that a company or individual offers, for payment, to create or restore wildlife habitat that offsets damage elsewhere. The developers seeking to offset their impact pay for the habitat work. The rule is balance or better: the biodiversity gained at the receptor site should equal or exceed the loss at the original site.

nature-mkt-125.title: Compensatory mitigation: the American name for offsetting
nature-mkt-125.text: In the United States, biodiversity offsetting goes by another name: compensatory mitigation. It means measures that restore, create, enhance or preserve wetlands to make up for damage that cannot be avoided. It applies only after the sequence of avoid, minimize, then compensate has been followed. It can happen on or next to the damaged area, or off-site. Besides banks, permit holders can pay into an approved fund, called an in-lieu fee program, or do and answer for the work themselves. Revised US rules in 2008 made mitigation banks the preferred method.

nature-mkt-126.title: Conservation easements: protection that runs with the land
nature-mkt-126.text: A conservation easement 'runs with the land': it binds present and future owners and is usually permanent. It is a voluntary legal agreement between a landowner and a government agency or conservation group that restricts future development on a site, setting it aside for conservation. In the US, land used for mitigation banking must be protected this way, and a trust fund may pay for long-term management. Landowners may see the permanent restriction as a drawback, since it limits future uses and can lower land value. Critics say easement tax deductions are abused to avoid tax, and US courts have penalized overstated easement values.

nature-mkt-131.title: Debits and credits for nature
nature-mkt-131.text: An environmental crediting system works like a ledger for nature. A governing body allocates debits for planned environmental damage and credits for conservation gains, so damage can be offset by buying credits. Credits come from banks where a resource has been improved; debits arise where significant harm is planned at a permitted site. Biodiversity banking in all its forms is an example. Three problems recur: choosing the unit of exchange, making debits and credits ecologically equivalent, and proving additionality. Some consider measuring biodiversity in such units impossible, or reject it on ethical grounds.

nature-mkt-133.title: Net positive impact: leaving nature better off
nature-mkt-133.text: No net loss aims to cancel out biodiversity loss. Net positive impact aims higher: a project's environmental gains from mitigation should outweigh its harms, leaving more biodiversity than before. Net gain is used in the same sense. England's Biodiversity Net Gain policy, for example, requires a 10% gain compared with the previous state. The two goals work at different scales. Net positive impact usually applies to a single development project, while no net loss is applied at many geographic scales.

nature-mkt-134.title: Offset ratios: paying back more than was taken
nature-mkt-134.text: Under a coverage ratio of 3:1, a developer must supply 3 compensatory mitigation credits for each unit of ecological damage. Mitigation ratios like this set how much habitat must be credited for each unit of harm. They have been proposed as a way to handle uncertainty in offsetting. Like-for-like rules add a second demand: offsets must match or exceed the biodiversity lost. Uganda's law requires offsets to be 'like-for-like or better', while China's eco-compensation does not. Friends of the Earth argues that like-for-like compensation of lost biodiversity may not be possible.

reviews.offsets-and-banking: This chapter traced one chain of logic from a principle to a market. Environmental mitigation and its hierarchy put offsetting last, after harm has been avoided, minimized and restored, and no net loss sets the goal of balancing what remains. Banking turns that goal into tradable credits, from more than 1200 US wetland mitigation banks to conservation banks for endangered species and credits aimed at extinction risk. Each step depends on hard measurement: a unit of exchange, equivalent debits and credits, ratios to cover uncertainty, and proof of additionality. The record so far is mixed, from US wetland banking that produced a net loss of area to the critics' charge that offsetting is a license to trash.
